LA PAZ, Bolivia (CNN)  -- Bolivian officials have declared a health emergency after three deaths attributed to dengue hemorrhagic fever, the often-lethal form of a mosquito-borne disease that more than 1,000 Bolivians are thought to have contracted since November. Brazilian soldiers pour insecticide to fight dengue fever in 2008. Bolivia also is battling the mosquito-borne disease. At least 12 unconfirmed instances of dengue hemorrhagic fever have been reported in the first 17 days of 2009, the official ABI news agency said. About 250 cases of dengue fever, the milder, nonlethal form of the disease, have been confirmed in the past two weeks, said Health Minister Ramiro Tapia in the Los Tiempos de Cochabamba newspaper. Authorities said they have committed more than 20,000 military personnel and 2.5 tons of insecticide to combat the disease. A preteen boy died last week at Children's Hospital of La Paz, a few days after arriving with internal bleeding, hospital director Christian Fuentes told La Razon newspaper in La Paz, the nation's capital. "By that time, there was nothing we could do. He had multiple internal hemorrhages," Fuentes said. A 17-year-old boy and a 30-year-old woman also died last week, the ABI news agency said, citing the national director of epidemiology, Juan Carlos Arraya. Cases of dengue fever usually spike from November through January, which is Bolivia's hot and rainy season. Alberto Nogales, the country's vice minister of health, said the fight against mosquitoes will last until April. Dengue occurs in tropical and subtropical parts of the world, transmitted by the bite of a mosquito infected with one of four dengue viruses, the World Health Organization says. Symptoms, which appear three to 14 days after the bite, can include mild to high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain and a rash, the WHO says. Dengue hemorrhagic fever is a potentially fatal complication that affects mainly children, the WHO says. Symptoms include fever, abdominal pain, vomiting and bleeding. The disease cannot be transmitted directly from one person to another. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates there are up to 100 million cases worldwide each year. "It actually is quite common," Dr. Ali Khan of the CDC told CNN last year. "And unfortunately, over the last 30 years or so we've seen an increase in the number of countries infected with dengue fever." Khan attributes the increase in part to population growth. Mosquitoes that carry dengue typically breed in areas near humans. "This is a disease that occurs where there's lots of population," he said. The WHO says mosquitoes carrying dengue viruses breed in exposed water, including places as shallow as jars, discarded bottles and plant saucers. Last year, 55,000 people in southeastern Brazil contracted the disease. The outbreak was confirmed as causing the deaths of at least 67 people -- almost half of them children under 13 -- and another 58 deaths were under investigation last summer, the Rio de Janeiro state's ministry of health reported at the time. Final statistics on the outbreak were not immediately available.

**LA PAZ, Bolivia (CNN)** — The Bolivian government declared a national health emergency on Tuesday as the country battles its worst outbreak of dengue fever in more than two decades, with thousands of people infected and hospitals overwhelmed.

Health officials reported that more than 30,000 suspected cases of the mosquito-borne virus have been registered since the beginning of the year, with at least 18 confirmed deaths linked to dengue hemorrhagic fever—the severe, potentially fatal strain of the disease.

The tropical eastern department of Santa Cruz has emerged as the epicenter of the crisis, accounting for more than 60% of all reported cases. Hospitals and emergency clinics in the region are running out of beds, forcing medical staff to treat patients in hallways and makeshift triage tents.

"We are facing an epidemiological crisis of unprecedented proportions in recent history," Bolivian Health Minister Ramiro Tapia told reporters in La Paz. "Declaring a state of emergency allows us to immediately release emergency funds and coordinate a unified national response."

### Military Deployed to Fight Mosquitos

President Evo Morales announced that thousands of military personnel are being deployed across the country to assist health workers in a massive containment effort. Troops will go door-to-door in affected areas to perform fumigation and help residents remove containers of standing water where the *Aedes aegypti* mosquito—the primary carrier of the virus—breeds.

Meteorologists attribute the severity of this year's outbreak to unusually heavy seasonal rainfall and high humidity, which have created ideal breeding conditions for mosquitoes across Bolivia’s lowlands. 

International assistance has begun to arrive. The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) and the World Health Organization (WHO) have dispatched epidemiologists and medical supplies to La Paz and Santa Cruz. Neighboring countries, including Cuba and Venezuela, have also offered specialized medical teams and insecticides.

### A Growing Regional Concern

Dengue fever, often called "breakbone fever" due to the intense muscle and joint pain it causes, presents with symptoms including high fever, severe headache, rash, and bodily aches. While most sufferers recover within a week, severe cases can lead to internal bleeding, organ failure, and death if not promptly treated with fluid management.

There is currently no specific antiviral treatment or widely available vaccine for dengue, making vector control—eliminating mosquito breeding grounds—the primary line of defense.

The rapid spread of the virus in Bolivia has put neighboring nations on high alert. Health authorities in northern Argentina, Paraguay, and western Brazil have heightened border surveillance and initiated localized spraying campaigns, fearing the outbreak could trigger a broader South American health crisis.

Bolivian health officials warn that the peak of the epidemic may still be weeks away as rain continues to fall across the region. They are urging citizens to use insect repellent, wear protective clothing, and report early symptoms immediately to nearby clinics.

**LA PAZ, Bolivia** — The Bolivian government has deployed the armed forces and declared a public health emergency as a severe outbreak of dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF) surges across the country, overburdening hospitals and claiming dozens of lives, primarily among children.

According to figures released Tuesday by the Ministry of Health, Bolivia has recorded more than 18,200 confirmed cases of dengue so far this year, with at least 58 confirmed deaths attributed to the severe hemorrhagic variant of the mosquito-borne virus. Health officials warn the actual numbers may be significantly higher due to underreporting in remote rural areas.

While the administrative capital of La Paz sits at an altitude too high for the *Aedes aegypti* mosquito to thrive, the crisis is being coordinated from the city as patients from the tropical lowlands of Santa Cruz, Beni, and the Yungas valleys are airlifted to high-complexity medical centers in the capital.

### Military Deployment and Field Hospitals

In response to the escalating crisis, President Luis Arce ordered the mobilization of thousands of military personnel to assist civilian health workers. Troops wearing protective gear and carrying motorized fogging equipment have been deployed across urban epicenters to conduct massive fumigation campaigns and drain standing water where mosquitoes breed.

"We are facing a health crisis that requires an immediate, national response," said Minister of Health María Renée Castro during a press briefing in La Paz. "The armed forces are not only helping us fumigate streets and clear breeding grounds, but they are also setting up mobile field hospitals and providing logistical support to transport critical patients from overwhelmed rural clinics to major cities."

At the Mario Ortiz Children's Hospital in Santa Cruz—the epicenter of the outbreak—pediatric wards are operating at more than 200% capacity. Doctors report treating multiple children in single beds, with makeshift triage centers set up in corridors.

"We are seeing a far higher proportion of patients presenting with severe symptoms than in previous years," said Dr. Carlos Hurtado, director of the regional health service in Santa Cruz. "Dengue hemorrhagic fever strikes fast. Within hours, a patient can go from a mild fever to internal bleeding and circulatory collapse. Our intensive care units are completely saturated."

### Understanding Dengue Hemorrhagic Fever: WHO and CDC Context

Dengue is an infection caused by one of four closely related dengue viruses (DEN-1, DEN-2, DEN-3, and DEN-4). According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), recovery from infection with one virus provides lifelong immunity against *that* specific serotype, but only temporary, partial protection against the other three. 

Crucially, the CDC warns that a second infection with a different dengue virus serotype significantly increases a person's risk of developing severe dengue, also known as Dengue Hemorrhagic Fever (DHF) or Dengue Shock Syndrome (DSS). 

The World Health Organization (WHO) notes that DHF is a potentially fatal complication characterized by:
*   Fever lasting two to seven days.
*   Severe abdominal pain and persistent vomiting.
*   Plasma leakage leading to fluid accumulation and respiratory distress.
*   Severe bleeding from the gums, nose, or under the skin (ecchymosis).
*   A sudden drop in blood pressure resulting in shock and organ failure.

Without proper medical care—primarily aggressive fluid replacement therapy and close monitoring—the mortality rate for severe dengue can exceed 20%. However, with early detection and specialized medical management, that rate can be reduced to less than 1%.

The WHO has warned that changing weather patterns linked to El Niño and global climate change have expanded the geographic range and breeding seasons of *Aedes* mosquitoes across Latin America. Higher temperatures accelerate the viral incubation period inside the mosquito, making the insects infectious much faster.

### Community Mobilization and Challenges Ahead

Beyond military intervention, the government has instituted mandatory "Cleanliness Days" (*Jornadas de Limpieza*) across affected municipalities, instructing residents to clear their yards of discarded tires, buckets, and open containers that collect rainwater.

Despite these efforts, health officials acknowledge that heavy seasonal rains are hampering control measures by washing away insecticide sprays and creating new breeding sites overnight.

"The military presence buys us time, but the ultimate solution relies on community action and sustained public health infrastructure," Castro said in La Paz. "We urge every family to take this threat seriously. If a child presents with high fever and sudden severe stomach pain, do not wait—seek immediate medical care."

International relief agencies, including the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), have begun shipping emergency medical supplies, pediatric fluid kits, and mosquito netting to La Paz to support the government's response.

**Bolivia Declares State of Emergency Over Deadly Dengue Outbreak; 20,000 Troops Deployed**

**LA PAZ, Bolivia** — The Bolivian government has declared a national state of emergency following a severe outbreak of dengue hemorrhagic fever that has killed at least three people and infected more than 1,000 others across the country. 

In a massive effort to contain the rapidly spreading mosquito-borne virus, officials have deployed 20,000 troops nationwide. Armed with industrial sprayers, military personnel are working alongside public health crews to conduct widespread insecticide fumigation, target high-risk neighborhoods, and assist overwhelmed healthcare facilities.

Public health officials report that the outbreak has escalated quickly, propelled by favorable weather conditions that have accelerated the growth of the local mosquito population.

### A Severe and Potentially Fatal Threat

According to the World Health Organization (WHO) and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), dengue is transmitted to humans through the bites of infected female mosquitoes, primarily the *Aedes aegypti* species. 

While standard dengue fever causes severe flu-like symptoms—including high fevers, debilitating muscle and joint pain (often called "breakbone fever"), severe headaches, and skin rashes—the situation in Bolivia is heightened by the prevalence of dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF). 

The CDC warns that DHF is a severe, potentially lethal complication. Symptoms of DHF usually begin after the initial fever subsides and include severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding from the gums or nose, blood in urine or stool, and subcutaneous bleeding that appears as bruising. Without immediate medical care and fluid management, DHF can cause severe blood loss, sudden drops in blood pressure (dengue shock syndrome), organ failure, and death.

### Target: Mosquito Breeding Grounds

Health authorities are focusing their emergency efforts on environmental control. The WHO notes that *Aedes aegypti* mosquitoes are highly adapted to urban environments and breed predominantly in man-made water containers. 

Common breeding sites include discarded tires, uncovered water storage drums, buckets, flowerpots, and blocked rain gutters. CDC guidelines highlight that female mosquitoes lay their eggs on the inner walls of water-filled containers, where the eggs can survive for months in dry conditions, hatching as soon as they are exposed to water.

Because there is no specific antiviral treatment for dengue, troops and health workers are prioritizing the elimination of these standing water sources while spraying insecticides to kill adult mosquitoes and disrupt the transmission cycle.

### Echoes of South America’s Dengue History

The crisis in Bolivia has drawn immediate comparisons to the historic 2008 dengue epidemic in neighboring Brazil, one of the worst outbreaks in South American history. During the 2008 surge, Brazil recorded over 500,000 cases and more than 200 deaths, with the state of Rio de Janeiro becoming the epicenter where field hospitals were erected to handle the influx of critical patients.

While Bolivia’s current count of over 1,000 infected individuals is substantially lower than Brazil's 2008 figures, experts warn that the high proportion of hemorrhagic cases poses an acute threat to Bolivia's medical infrastructure. Public health experts emphasize that swift military intervention and early public cooperation are essential if Bolivia is to avoid a catastrophe on the scale seen in Brazil sixteen years ago.

Bolivian health officials continue to urge citizens to clear standing water from their homes, use insect repellent, wear protective clothing, and seek immediate medical attention at the first sign of severe dengue symptoms.

According to figures from the Bolivian Ministry of Health and the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the current outbreak cycle has seen tens of thousands of suspected cases, with confirmed infections rapidly climbing. Tragically, the body count includes a disproportionate number of children. 

"We are seeing an alarming rate of Severe Dengue—formerly known as dengue hemorrhagic fever," said Dr. Elena Mendoza, an infectious disease specialist working at a public hospital in Santa Cruz. "Patients, particularly minors, are arriving with severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, and internal bleeding. Many families wait too long to seek care because early symptoms mirror a common flu."

Local health authorities report that intensive care unit (ICU) beds across public hospitals have reached near-100% capacity. Emergency responders have set up temporary tents outside major hospitals to screen patients, attempting to filter mild cases away from overcrowded emergency rooms.

---

### **The Perfect Storm: Seasonal and Environmental Causes**

Dengue is a viral infection transmitted to humans through the bite of infected female *Aedes aegypti* mosquitoes. The current crisis in Bolivia is the result of a compounding set of seasonal, environmental, and infrastructural factors.

1. **Intense Rainy Season and High Humidity:** Bolivia’s rainy season—which typically runs from November to April—creates ideal breeding conditions for mosquitoes. Heavy torrential rains leave behind countless pockets of stagnant water in urban and rural environments alike, from discarded tires and flowerpots to unsealed water storage drums.
2. **The El Niño Phenomenon:** Unusually high temperatures accelerated by the El Niño climate pattern have shortened the incubation period of the virus inside the mosquito and increased the insect's biting frequency. Higher temperatures also cause mosquito larvae to develop faster, exponentially increasing the vector population.
3. **Rapid, Unplanned Urbanization:** Cities like Santa Cruz have expanded rapidly over the last two decades. In many informal settlements, reliable municipal water infrastructure is lacking. Residents are forced to store water in large open containers, unwittingly creating ideal nurseries for *Aedes aegypti*, a species that thrives in close proximity to human dwellings.

"Climate change is no longer a distant threat for South America; it is a present health emergency," said Carlos Vargas, an environmental epidemiologist based in La Paz. "The geographic zones where the mosquito can survive are expanding higher into the valleys, putting populations with no historical immunity at risk."

---

### **The Global Picture: A World Under Threat**

Bolivia’s emergency is not an isolated event. It is a microcosm of a staggering global surge in vector-borne diseases. 

According to the World Health Organization (WHO), dengue is the fastest-spreading mosquito-borne disease in the world today. The global statistics paint a worrying picture:

* **Exponential Growth:** Global dengue cases have increased **eight-fold over the last two decades**, rising from roughly 500,000 cases in 2000 to over 5 million in recent peak years.
* **Global Burden:** The WHO estimates that approximately **half of the world's population**—around 4 billion people—is now at risk of dengue infection. An estimated **100 to 400 million infections** occur each year, though up to 80% are mild or asymptomatic.
* **The Americas Epicenter:** The Pan American Health Organization reported a record-breaking year for the Americas recently, with over **4.5 million cases and more than 2,300 deaths** recorded across Latin America and the Caribbean. Neighboring Brazil, Peru, and Argentina have also declared state health emergencies due to unprecedented outbreaks.
* **Creeping Geographic Reach:** Due to global warming, *Aedes* mosquitoes are expanding their footprint. Autochthonous (locally acquired) dengue cases are now regularly reported in non-traditional areas, including Southern Europe (France, Italy, Spain) and parts of the southern United States (Florida, Texas, California).

---

### **The Response and the Road Ahead**

In response to the domestic crisis, the Bolivian government, supported by international aid organizations, has deployed military personnel and health workers to conduct massive "clean-up days" (*mingas*). Troops have gone door-to-door in Santa Cruz to destroy mosquito breeding sites, apply larvicides to standing water, and conduct large-scale chemical fumigation in high-risk neighborhoods.

Despite these efforts, health experts emphasize that reactive measures are not enough. Vaccines against dengue, such as the newly approved *Qdenga*, offer hope, but global supply constraints and high procurement costs mean mass vaccination campaigns remain out of reach for many developing nations in the immediate term.

"Fumigation kills the adult mosquito today, but if there is standing water, new mosquitoes will hatch tomorrow," Dr. Mendoza warned, tending to a feverish child in her clinic. "Until we address urban infrastructure, poverty, and global climate trends, we will be back in this same emergency room, fighting the same battle, year after year."

For now, the people of Bolivia remain on high alert, scanning the skies for rain and hoping the end of the wet season will bring relief to a nation weary of disease.

***

*Report compiled with inputs from the World Health Organization (WHO), the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), and the Ministry of Health of Bolivia.*
